# National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) – Summary
The National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), founded in 1910 by Justo Sierra, is Mexico’s premier public university and one of Latin America’s largest and most prestigious educational institutions. Secular and national in scope, UNAM was created to unify decentralized colleges and promote liberal, positivist, and modern education. Over time, it gained autonomy, developed a robust academic structure, and played a significant role in Mexican history and politics, including advocacy for minority rights and political activism. Its motto, "For my people the spirit shall speak," and emblem featuring a double-headed eagle over Latin America, reflect its cultural and humanistic mission.
UNAM’s main campus, Ciudad Universitaria in Mexico City, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and includes notable museums and facilities such as the Palacio de Minería, National Biodiversity Pavilion, Museum of San Ildefonso, Chopo University Museum, and the National Astronomical Observatory. The university also has satellite campuses and international extensions. Academically, UNAM offers a comprehensive range of undergraduate and graduate programs through numerous schools and national colleges, and maintains one of the world’s largest student bodies (over 324,000). Renowned for research, UNAM excels in fields such as artificial intelligence, robotics, and the sciences, housing many leading research institutes and responsible for a significant share of Mexico’s scientific output. UNAM supports open and distance education options for thousands of students.
Notable for its cultural traditions, active student associations, and athletic teams such as Club Universidad Nacional (Pumas), UNAM alumni and faculty include Nobel laureates (Alfonso García Robles, Octavio Paz, Mario Molina), world leaders, prominent scientists, artists, and influential business figures like Carlos Slim. Throughout its history, UNAM has maintained a strong commitment to autonomy, inclusion, and the advancement of knowledge, culture, and social progress in Mexico and beyond.
